Under the [b]direct[/b] command of their self-proclaimed [b]Emir, Hassan Al-Amin[/b], ISV has [i]launched a brutal campaign[/i] known as Operation [b]Nur-Al-Deen[/b], a systematic effort to "[b]purify[/b]" the Republic by targeting [u]Shia communities, foreign-born/foreign working citizens, and refugee populations[/u].
[b]Thousands[/b] have ran to their homes as ISV forces continue advancing through wild sectors, [b]executing civilians and sacking towns[/b] that resist their [u]rule[/u].

Humanitarian reports [b]displacements[/b], with thousands of refugees moving north towards [u]Bakr City and Fahd city[/u], seeking more [b]safe[/b] cities.[/spoiler]

[Spoiler=Operation Amaal Al-waatan]In response to the [b]atrocities[/b] and the continued fall of [b]key territories[/b], Acting Commander and interim national leader, [b]Nadir Suleiman,[/b] has announced Operation [i]Amaal Al-Waatan[/i] [b](Hope of the Homeland).[/b]

This military [u]operation[/u] wants to retake the city of [b]Therene[/b], the [b]nations second-largest [u]urban[/u] center[/b] and an important [i]industrial[/i] hub that fell under ISV control earlier in the rise of the civil [b]war[/b].

[b]Valdderan socialist forces[/b], reinforced by [b]armored vehicles and air divisions from the western command,[/b] have begun [u]pushing[/u] southward along the [b]Vald and Therene axis.[/b]
Skirmishes are the [i]current tactics[/i], with [b]early reports of heavy resistance and high casualties on both sides[/b]. As military and [i]humanitarian[/i] aid is offered by various countries.[/spoiler]

Trade and military goes through the Shamat Sea have been [b]disrupted[/b], [i]endangering[/i] international [u]commerce[/u].
In response, [b]United Hydronia[/b], neighboring maritime partners, ports of both [b]Valdderan and Hydronic owned territories[/b] have been briefly [u]blockaded[/u] by the [b]ISV[/b] earlier in the war.

[b]Arenenge lands on Valdderan shores[/b]

- - - The Arenese navy , after having a surprisingly smooth way through the seas, have finally reached the cost of Valddera. The navy sent out three transport vehicles with marines ready to kill terrorists, and used their on-board artillery to cover the marines while they landed. The marines started to set up fortifications on the shore, while the Arenese navy and Valdderan Islamic Extremists fought. The marines, particularly feeling uneasy that day, had a slightly slower response and didnt take the shores quite as easy as in the plans. Though they persisted. The Arenese military contacted the Valdderan Government, and told them of their arrival. The Arenese's first mission was to cover the shores. This is to keep anyone from supplying the Islamic Extremists, and allowing the innocent civillians to flee or temporarily hide under Arenese protection. 

[b]Arenese Operations[/b]

- - - A couple hours later, the fight died down. The Army was now authorized to be sent, and the marines had cleared only a fraction of the coastlines. The Arenese army would have the upper hand in this war, not only because of their air and naval superiority, but because of their strategic knowledge. The Arenese military had sent spies prior to the war, and gained information about the land, and some of the enemy's bases. The Valderran Military would also accompany the Arenese Liberation Army to give them key intel on some locations and terrain to further help them in the war. This wasn't going to be easy, but none the less, the Valdderan people are strong.

- - - The Arenese Army sent out two teams of reconnaissance troops, a company of about 15 each. [i]"Squad Borderlings"[/i] will scout along the borders of Valddera. [i]"Squad Sand Scrapers"[/i] would glide across the coastline. [i]"Squad Central"[/i] would maneuver the land infront of them. Five members of each team would be equipped with an HK416, chosen for their range. Seven members would be equipped with a SIG MPX, a small sub-machine gun chosen for their smaller mass. And three members would be equipped with M110 SASS, a marksman rifle designed for swift eliminations. All equipment was chosen for agility and speed, because these teams were not meant to get into a firefight, they were meant to assassinate, be swift, and relay information.

[i][b]September 1-6, 2026 Operation Spearhead.[/b]

Operation Spearhead, conducted from September 1 to September 6, 2026, was the United States of Oceanics decisive amphibious campaign to retake six rebel-held islands off Tallisland. The plan, authorized by President Ironvisak Willham and Supreme General Armin Vakus Lavaki, placed the 1st Carrier Strike Group and an Amphibious Expeditionary Force at the center of a tightly sequenced suppression, seizure, and stabilization operation. The campaign began with a concentrated suppression window on the morning of September 1 from 04:55 to 11:58. Carrier and strike assets, supported by maritime patrols and drones, executed precision strikes against rebel bases, command nodes, and known militia emplacements while explicitly avoiding populated town centers per ROE. Special Forces teams of S.D.S. were tasked to infiltrate and secure high-value targets immediately after the suppression phase, while amphibious and heliborne assault waves followed to establish lodgments on each island. The operation assumed a committed assault and consolidation force of roughly 31,200 personnel, about 25,000 assault and follow on troops including roughly 15,000 marines and amphibious forces, 1,200 Special Forces operators, and 5,000 peacekeeping and stabilization troops staged to secure gains.

Island Alpha, the largest and highest-priority objective, was estimated to host approximately 1,800 rebel fighters with two hardened compounds and a civilian town of some 2,000 people in the north. During the opening strikes the carrier wing and supporting surface fires suppressed the rebel compounds and caches to the east and north of the town while EW denied rebel communications. S.D.S. teams inserted at 09:30 to seize and secure the island airfield and interdicted command communications; at 12:30 the first amphibious wave struck the west beach while mechanized support the airlifted to the captured airfield. By the evening of September 1, USO forces held the main port and runway; consolidated clearing operations continued into September 2 and the island was declared operationally secure by September 3. Rebel remnants numbered in the low hundreds and either fled inland or surrendered; infrastructure damage was limited and peacekeeping units established checkpoints and humanitarian corridors.
Island Bravo was a secondary population center where some 1,200 militia fighters had fortified small towns and rocket positions. Precision strikes neutralized three compound clusters and two rocket emplacements before amphibious landings in the late morning and mechanized pushes into town that afternoon. Urban fighting was intense but relatively short; the town was cleared by September 2 with estimated rebel casualties in the low hundreds and USO losses light but real, roughly two dozen killed and several times that wounded. Peacekeepers moved in on September 3 to secure and administer aid.

Island Charlie was the campaigns most difficult objective, a rugged island with an estimated 3,500 fighters, several mobile anti-ship missile sites, and deep inland strongpoints. The suppression window concentrated on suspected missile emplacements and staging areas to reduce the threat to approaching ships and landing craft, and S.D.S. teams were heavily tasked with locating and disabling SAM and anti-ship systems. Diversionary amphibious landings were used while main heliborne assaults attempted to seize inland plateaus, but the rebels exploited caves, ridgelines, and prepared positions to bloody the advance. Charlie remained contested through the operations end, with USO forces securing coastal towns and ports but persistent interior resistance forcing prolonged clearing operations. This island produced the campaigns heaviest price: USO casualties on Charlie were the largest single-island toll, with total USO KIA across the campaign estimated in the mid-hundreds and wounded in the low thousands, most of the dead and wounded occurring on Charlie. Rebel losses on Charlie were severe as well but many fighters dispersed into the interior to wage an insurgency beyond the six-day window.

Island Delta, smaller but possessing an airstrip, was handled as a high-value logistics objective. Limited strikes on coastal batteries and the comm node enabled a morning helicopter insertion to the airfield and a southern amphibious landing in the early afternoon. Engineers worked through the night to repair and mark the runway; by dawn the next day C-130s were operating into the field with resupply and casualty evacuation. Delta rapidly became a forward logistics hub that shortened sustainment lines for the rest of the operation.
Island Echo presented a delicate challenge because of high civilian density in fishing towns. The operational directive to avoid strikes in population centers shaped a cautious approach: targeted strikes hit ammunition dumps and rebel dockside warehouses in the morning while amphibious landings took place in preselected, unpopulated surf zones at midday. A robust civil affairs presence accompanied the assault battalion to shepherd civilians into humanitarian corridors and to begin immediate relief distributions. By September 4 Echo was largely cleared of organized rebel resistance and under peacekeeping control, though displacement and humanitarian need were significant.
Island Foxtrot, an outlying relay island used by the rebels to link the other islands, held only some 400 fighters and was the quickest objective to secure. An early strike package suppressed coastal positions and a fast S.D.S. heliborne seizure of the radio mast and port at mid-morning unhinged the rebel communications link. Amphibious forces landed before noon and the island was cleared by evening, quickly repurposed as a staging base for follow-on logistics and overwatch.

Across the six-island operation the USO committed a balanced mix of assets of amphibious brigades and mechanized companies totaling roughly 25,000 assault and immediate follow-on troops, approximately 1,200 Special Forces operators distributed to exploit and secure high-value nodes, and some 5,000 peacekeepers and stabilization personnel staged to arrive as areas were cleared. The vehicle package assigned to the operation included roughly 222 IFVs and amphibious fighting vehicles, approximately 72 APCs, some 36 self-propelled artillery pieces with supplementary HIMARS batteries at theater level, and about 62 attack helicopters for close air support, escort, and armed reconnaissance. Carrier air wings conducted an estimated 120 strike sorties during the opening suppression window and provided persistent CAP and SEAD through the first 48 hours; naval surface combatants provided shore bombardment and fires support while an amphibious squadron of LHD/LPD/LST ships executed the ship-to-shore movement and RO/RO vessels handled heavier equipment and sustainment loads.

By the conclusion of the named operation phase on September 6, operational control had been established on five of the six target islands: Alpha, Bravo, Delta, Echo, and Foxtrot were held and transitioned to peacekeeping duties in the immediate aftermath. Island Charlie remained the campaigns most stubborn pocket of resistance, secured along its coasts but with interior strongpoints that required extended counterinsurgency operations. Rebel command-and-control had been severely degraded by the combined cyber and kinetic campaign that preceded the landings, and estimates place rebel casualties and captures in the several thousands across all islands. USO combat losses for the period were painful but within the bounds of what planners anticipated for a forcible entry: estimates in this plan place KIA in the mid-hundreds and wounded in the low thousands, with the highest rates concentrated on Island Charlie; a small number of helicopters and landing craft were lost or damaged in the kinetic phase.

Civilian harm was minimized where possible but unavoidable in several sectors; infrastructure damage affected power, docks, and local services, and substantial displacement occurred on Echo and Alpha. Humanitarian corridors and emergency aid were prioritized as islands were secured, with engineers and medics working to restore runways and medical facilities for faster relief delivery. Strategically, Operation Spearhead achieved its objective of severing the rebels inter-island coordination and denying them island sanctuaries, but the protracted fight on the interior of Charlie signaled that the campaign would shift from a short, sharp amphibious seizure into a longer stabilization and counterinsurgency phase. Politically the operation delivered a tactical victory for President Willham and the USO, but it also sparked intense international scrutiny and a debate at home about the costs of occupation, the pace of reconstruction, and the long-term plan to transition authority back to stable Tallisland institutions.
